purpose: reader-facing explanation of the market categories, skills, and responsibility layers found in AI Engineer job descriptions

required_facts.fact: The study analyzed 1,000+ job descriptions and classified 889 into three categories.
required_facts.evidence: Source lines 3 and 6: dataset size and classification count are stated.

required_facts.fact: AI-first roles were about 70 percent and worked on LLM/GenAI systems, RAG, agents, evaluation, and production deployment.
required_facts.evidence: Source line 8: category and responsibilities are specified.

required_facts.fact: AI-support roles were about 28.5 percent and focused on infrastructure and platforms around AI.
required_facts.evidence: Source line 9: support category and examples are listed.

required_facts.fact: Traditional ML/DL roles were under 2 percent and used standard ML or deep-learning tools under the AI Engineer title.
required_facts.evidence: Source line 10: category and tool examples are described.

required_facts.fact: The practical definition was an engineer owning foundation-model system design, evaluation, and production operation.
required_facts.evidence: Source line 14: market-driven definition is stated.

required_facts.fact: The roles were 95.6 percent production-focused, nearly 50 percent backend-heavy, and 20 percent often full-stack.
required_facts.evidence: Source line 16: production and application-layer statistics are given.

required_facts.fact: The leading GenAI signals were RAG at 35.9 percent, prompt engineering at 29.1 percent, LLM integration at 25.4 percent, agents at 14.4 percent, and fine-tuning at 8.5 percent.
required_facts.evidence: Source lines 25-29: skill mentions are listed.

required_facts.fact: Python was mentioned in 82.5 percent of roles, with TypeScript, React, and FastAPI also appearing.
required_facts.evidence: Source lines 35-38: language and app-layer signals are described.

required_facts.fact: Operations and cloud were mentioned in 17.4 and 13.4 percent of postings, while AWS, Docker, CI/CD, and Kubernetes formed a common infrastructure baseline.
required_facts.evidence: Source lines 40-44 and 56-60: operations, cloud, and tooling signals are stated.

required_facts.fact: Day-to-day work had core, common, and secondary layers, ranging from end-to-end RAG and agents to proprietary retrieval, platforms, frontend work, fine-tuning, and security.
required_facts.evidence: Source lines 71-77: responsibility layers and evolving core are described.

author_attribution: Explain the dataset's signals and qualifications without turning its percentages into universal guarantees or prescribing a specific framework.
